rv.q: Things pick up after the interval when a garishly dressed Broderick, suddenly bearing a startling resemblance to Austin Powers, portrays a Hollywood producer intent on seducing his high school girlfriend.
Sarah Jessica Parker's London theatre debut is dazzling
The public appetite for this show...stems greatly from Parker's presence.
Before it, though, Plaza Suite is really quite a treat.
The main draw of John Benjamin Hickey's production is the evident bond between Parker and Broderick as they play out multiple variations of marital misery.
The jokes feel effortful and small 'c' conservative
...it’s a theatrical museum piece, barely in working order, dusty and decidedly creaky.
The production seems effectively to coast on the fame of its two stars.
I could not wait to check out of Plaza Suite.
Matthew Broderick and Sarah Jessica Parker...are doing coathanger acting, encased in a set by John Lee Beatty that is both doggedly realistic and flimsy.
The biggest takeaway is just what a brilliant stage performer Parker is, whether landing a wry zinger with expert precision or letting loose in some fantastic physical comedy.

As a play, Plaza Suite is showing signs of its age, it won’t have audiences rolling in the aisles but it does have enough to raise a few smiles and a couple of good laughs. But its star cast does make this one of the West End’s unmissable shows, primarily because Sarah Jessica Parker brings sublimity to the city in this powerhouse performance.

Sarah Jessica Parker's screen renown as Carrie Bradshaw in Sex and the City has made a London event out of the West End revival of Plaza Suite, the Neil Simon triptych from 1968 that is as definably New York as the TV series in which Parker made her name.
Overall, an enjoyable night with the stars.
Escapism we need, too, but it doesn't warrant the ticket prices—poof and it's gone. It's a blancmange.
Overall, this revival is a mixed bag with a glittering exterior. It is lavish, starry and it oozes class, but it also carries several reminders that all that glitters is not gold.
The dialogue sounds true to life but it's also meandering, flat and witless – the sort of drivel you'd overhear in a vet's waiting room.
Even though I chuckled throughout, the more I thought about it all afterwards, the less funny I found it.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this star-powered revival: some find Parker and Broderick's chemistry delightful in Simon's triptych, while others deem the 1968 comedy dated and the eye-watering ticket prices hard to justify.
